newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Interview-NZ's Lion to diversify or buy back stock.
newsitem.headline: Interview-NZ's Lion to diversify or buy back stock.

text.p: Lion Nathan Ltd chief executive Douglas Myers said on Wednesday that the future cash flow of the brewer would be directed toward diversification into other countries such as China, where it already had a presence, or returned to shareholders in the form of share buybacks.

Myers told Reuters the future of Lion, ranked fifth in terms of total market capitalisation in New Zealand, lay not in the mature markets of Australasia but in the Asia-Pacific region, particularly China, where the company was pleased with its run in the Yangtze River Delta region over the last 12-18 months.
Lion has an 80 percent interest in the Lion Nathan Taihushui Brewery in Wuxi and has started work on a wholly owned "greenfields" plant in nearby Suzhou, due for completion in two years.
Suzhou would have an initial production capacity of 200 million litres a year, with potential for 400 million litres.
The plant for Suzhou was bought before tariffs on imported machinery were put in place, giving the company an advantage over any new entrants.
On the negative side, China is proposing to re-invigorate its domestic brewing industry through preferential loans and trading conditions for 10 leading operators.
"Our understanding is that we will not be competing head-to-head with any of them. None of that is going to worry us in the immediate term," he said.
If China does change the rules, it may turn to Lion's advantage.

"I mean, if you want to come in to our part of the woods now: one, you're going to have to pay a lot more because of all these tariff changes; secondly, it's going to be very much more difficult to do it; thirdly, in Suzhou we have a 100 percent-owned brewery...and again, they have said they do not want any more 100 percent-owned ventures," he said.
Myers said Lion was in informal talks with two other brewers in the region with a view to possible joint ventures.
In the meantime, Wuxi and Suzhou were enough to keep the company busy.
Lion has been repaying debt at an average rate of NZ$150 million a year over the last five years after a highly leveraged purchase of brewing assets from the now defunct Bond Corp.
This would, in time, lead to a credit rating upgrade that would again raise the question of a return of capital to shareholders.

"But it's more a matter of fleshing out the structure that we have now established in a strategic sense which, over time, will give us other options in terms of what we are going to do with the surplus cash," Myers said.
"What we are not going to do is invest any more money back into beer into Australia or New Zealand -- we've done that," he said.
